meta.title: This Country Redrew the Map So It Could Share One Calendar Day
meta._convention: Duration omitted per beat -- filled from measured narration length. Kiribati (KI) is in country-codes.json but is NOT present in the world-atlas 110m countries dataset (confirmed by direct node lookup against countries-110m.json), so highlight stays [] throughout -- markers/lines carry the whole visual, per the 'scenes that aren't a country' pattern. IMPORTANT (verified empirically against fitBBoxProjection): d3-geo's fitExtent/bounds math NORMALIZES any longitude outside -180..180 back into that range before computing the ring's winding/area, so a camera bbox that crosses the antimeridian (east<west after normalization, e.g. [172,-10]-[212,10], OR the plain west>east form [172,-10]-[-157,10]) collapses to a broken whole-world scale, NOT a tight regional crop -- confirmed by direct fitBBoxProjection() calls returning scale~140 (whole-world) instead of a real crop for both forms. There is no continuous-longitude workaround: every beat's camera.from/camera.to here therefore stays strictly on ONE side of +/-180 (Gilbert Islands beats use positive lon up to 179.9; Line Islands beats use negative lon from -179.9), while markers/lines use TRUE unmodified real-world lon/lat (e.g. Kiritimati stays -157.4, not +202.6) -- point projection (unlike fitExtent's bounds calc) normalizes correctly on its own, confirmed via direct d3-geo projection calls, so markers always land in their correct real position under whichever one-sided camera is active. Real-world reference: Tarawa/Gilbert Islands ~172.98E,1.33N; old date line ran along 180 degrees; Kiritimati (Christmas Island) ~-157.4,1.87N; Millennium/Caroline Island ~-150.2,-9.94 (first land on Earth to see each new day).

beats.voText: This country spans more than a thousand miles of Pacific Ocean, so far, its own calendar used to split down the middle.
It's called Kiribati, dozens of islands stretching from the Gilbert Islands to the Line Islands, almost a third of the way around the globe.
The date line used to run straight through the country, putting its eastern islands a full calendar day behind the west.
beats.onScreenText: The date line cut it in half.

beats.voText: In 1995, Kiribati simply redrew the map, bending the date line east, around its own islands, so the whole country shared one single day.
Now its easternmost islands sit fourteen hours ahead of New York, making Kiribati the very first place on Earth to greet each new day.
beats.onScreenText: First to see each new day.

beats.voText: One country moved the actual date line just to share a calendar with itself, and now it's the first place on Earth to see tomorrow. Follow for more places on Earth that shouldn't exist, but do.
